e29613ba3d.q: What are the main ways dental practices leave money on the table according to Advanced Practice Management?
e29613ba3d.a: Practices often have high production but poor collections at the front desk, resulting in unbilled claims, uncollected monies, and high aging accounts receivable. They may send out huge amounts of statements and have large write-off or adjustment amounts. Kimberly Radke emphasizes that feeling busy does not mean the practice is actually collecting revenue, and there are solutions both at the front desk and clinically to improve collections as a team.

47c030e106.q: Should dental practices drop their PPO insurance plans to become fee-for-service?
47c030e106.a: Kimberly Radke advises against making an emotional decision to drop PPO plans. She recommends practices first run reports and understand their write-offs, and critically, know whether they are in or out of network—noting that she estimates nine and a half out of ten dentists don't know this. Practices should strategically evaluate whether dropping insurance is the right move only if they are at capacity, have huge write-offs, and have carefully analyzed their plan participation. Dropping plans without this analysis often results in significant patient loss.

c637e576cd.q: What is Advanced Practice Management's approach to dental staff retention beyond salary increases?
c637e576cd.a: Kimberly Radke emphasizes that retention requires clear systems, good communication through checklists, clearly defined roles and responsibilities, and real team building—not just social events. She uses DISC personality assessment to help teams understand each other's communication styles and work together. She also notes that simply throwing money at staff through salary increases is no longer effective because it is extremely expensive, so practices must take a step back and evaluate everything holistically.

abd98f2cb0.q: When should a dental practice hire a consultant according to Advanced Practice Management?
abd98f2cb0.a: Kimberly Radke recommends engaging a consultant when a practice is working harder but making less, writing off more, has flat collections, staff burnout, and staff turnover. However, she also notes success comes from good practices that want to become great practices and are willing to invest in systems before reaching a crisis. Consultants can be engaged at any point—front end, middle, or end—depending on the practice's readiness and goals.
